extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, applicants, attorneys/agents, and USPTO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the duty of disclosure (37 CFR 1.56 and related rules) for information material to patentability, including what must be disclosed, who must disclose, how and when to disclose, remedies after grant, and best practices to ensure compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of information from litigation or trial proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject matter for which a patent is being sought is, or has been, involved in litigation and/or a trial proceeding, or the litigation and/or trial proceeding yields information material to currently pending applications, the existence of such litigation and any other material information arising therefrom must be brought to the attention of the examiner or other appropriate official at the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material litigation information should be submitted on an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS). Examples of such material information include evidence of possible prior public use or sales, questions of inventorship, prior art, allegations of "fraud," "inequitable conduct," and "violation of duty of disclosure," and any assertion in litigation that contradicts assertions made to the examiner. For reissue applications, litigation that raises questions material to reissue (e.g., validity, fraud, inequitable conduct) must be disclosed at filing or promptly thereafter, and relevant litigation documents should accompany the application when material to patentability as defined in 37 CFR 1.56.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification required when claims are copied from a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claims are copied or substantially copied from a patent, 37 CFR 41.202(a) requires the applicant, at the time he or she presents the claim(s), to identify the patent and the numbers of the patent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The information required by 37 CFR 41.202(a) as to the source of copied claims is material information under 37 CFR 1.56 and failure to inform the USPTO may violate the duty of disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of regulatory review documentation (e.g., FDA) when material
rubrics_metrics.description: Where relevant documentation is submitted to a regulatory review body, such as FDA, and is material to any pending patent application or reexamination proceeding, such documentation should be submitted for Office review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although FDA considerations differ from USPTO patentability determinations, submissions (particularly assertions contradictory to assertions made to the examiner) may be material. A duty of reasonable inquiry may require reviewing documents submitted to other government agencies and submitting any that are material. If the applicant intends to list a patent in the Orange Book and the filing date is after FDA marketing approval, consider informing the USPTO of that intent and providing the Paragraph IV factual and legal basis notice to USPTO. See Belcher Pharmaceuticals v. Hospira and MPEP § 2164.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to perform a reasonable inquiry before presenting papers to the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party presenting a paper to the USPTO has a duty to perform an inquiry that is reasonable under the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reasonable inquiry may include reviewing documents received from other government agencies. Failing to inquire when circumstances warrant it could result in sanctions under 37 CFR 11.18(c), including striking the paper, referral for disciplinary action, preclusion from submitting papers, affecting the weight of the paper, or terminating proceedings. See In re Hao and MPEP § 2015.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may satisfy the duty of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals other than the attorney, agent or inventor may comply with the duty by disclosing information to the attorney, agent, or inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.56(d) allows disclosure to the Office through an attorney or agent of record or through a pro se inventor; other individuals may satisfy their duty by providing the information to such attorney/agent/inventor who then is responsible for disclosure. Information that is not material need not be passed along to the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosures must be in writing and filed in each relevant file
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure under 37 CFR 1.56 must be in writing as prescribed by 37 CFR 1.2, and a copy of any such disclosure must be filed in each application or other proceeding to which the disclosure pertains (37 CFR 1.4(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All business with the PTO should be transacted in writing; the Office acts based exclusively on the written record. Each file must be complete in itself, so a separate copy of every paper must be furnished for each file to which the paper pertains; avoid filing duplicate copies except when required. Presentation of any paper constitutes a certification under § 11.18(b). 37 CFR 11.18(b)(2) calls for a duty of reasonable inquiry that the paper is not presented for improper purpose and factual contentions have evidentiary support.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) will be considered (timing rules under 37 CFR 1.97)
rubrics_metrics.description: An IDS will be considered by the Office during pendency if filed within one of the specified time periods in 37 CFR 1.97(b), or later if accompanied by required statements/fees as set forth in paragraphs (c), (d), and (e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IDS considered as a matter of right if filed: (1) within three months of filing a national application (other than CPA under §1.53(d)); (2) within three months of date of entry of national stage under §1.491; (3) before mailing of first Office action on the merits; (4) before mailing of first Office action after RCE under §1.114; (5) within three months of publication of international registration in certain design apps. IDS filed later may be considered if filed before final action/notice of allowance/closure and accompanied by the statement in paragraph (e) or fee under §1.17(p). Paragraph (e) requires certification about timing relative to foreign patent office citations or reasonable inquiry that items were not known more than three months prior to filing. In any circumstance, information should be submitted promptly and ideally before the first Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early submission and promptness principle
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant, attorney, or agent who is aware of material prior art or other information and its significance should submit the information as early as possible in prosecution, e.g., before the first Office action, and not wait until after allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potentially material information discovered late should be promptly submitted; paying the issue fee is no excuse for failing to submit information. Consider incentives for prompt filing (37 CFR 1.704(d)(1)). The presumption of validity is stronger when prior art was before and considered by the Office and weaker when it was not (see Bolkcom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means for bringing information to the Office after patent grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-grant, information may be brought to the Office by: (I) citations of prior art and written statements under 37 CFR 1.501; (II) ex parte reexamination (37 CFR 1.510); (III) supplemental examination (37 CFR 1.601-1.625); and (IV) reissue applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.501 entries are limited to prior art patents, printed publications, or patent owner written statements filed by the owner in court/Office proceedings. Ex parte reexamination allows third parties or patentees to request reconsideration based on patents/printed publications. Supplemental examination allows broader "information" (sales invoices, transcripts, etc.) and any ground of patentability, and can insulate a patent from unenforceability under 35 U.S.C. 257 if information is considered/reconsidered/corrected during supplemental examination. Reissue can be used to bring prior art or incorrect/inconsistent positions to the Office for a pending matter such as a reissue application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental examination scope and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplemental examination is not limited to patents, printed publications, and patent owner written statements; the information may include any information the patent owner believes relevant, and may involve any ground of patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information examples include patent, journal article, sales invoice, audio/video transcript. 35 U.S.C. 257(c)(1) provides that a patent shall not be held unenforceable on basis of conduct relating to information that had not been considered if that information was considered/reconsidered/corrected during supplemental examination. See MPEP Chapter 2800.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use letters, questionnaires, and checklists as compliance aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Many attorneys use letters and questionnaires for applicants and others, and checklists for themselves and applicants to ensure compliance with the duty of disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters should explain the duty of disclosure; questionnaires ask about origin of invention, point of departure from prior art, possible public uses and sales, prior publications, knowledge, patents, foreign patents, etc. Checklists help ensure the applicant has been informed of the duty and that the attorney has inquired of and cited material prior art. These aids are helpful though not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry and documentation about inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask questions about inventorship: who is the proper inventor, and whether disputes or possible disputes exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are questions, call them to the attention of the USPTO. It's desirable to record such inquiries and to ensure all individuals who may be subject to the duty are informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode inquiry and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask questions of the inventor about disclosure of the best mode and make sure that the best mode is described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2165 - 2165.04 for detailed discussion. Attorneys should ensure the best mode is described in the specification when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language oath/declaration comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever an individual making an oath or declaration cannot understand English, the oath or declaration must be in a language that the individual can understand and shall state that such individual understands the content of any documents to which the oath or declaration relates (37 CFR 1.69(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure foreign inventors recognize responsibilities in signing oath/declaration; provide translations or language-appropriate documents as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate prior art against the broadest reasonable interpretation of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully evaluate and explain to the applicant the scope of the claims, particularly the broadest claims; pick out the broadest claim(s) and measure the materiality of prior art against a reasonably broad interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mistakenly evaluating prior art in light of the gist or a narrower interpretation of the invention; focus on whether prior art is material to the broadest claim interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess materiality from viewpoint of closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be useful to evaluate the materiality of prior art or other information from the viewpoint of whether it is the closest prior art or other information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A withheld reference may be highly material when it discloses a more complete combination of relevant features, even if those features appear in other references. Consider whether a reference provides a more complete combination of elements claimed (Semiconductor Energy Laboratory v. Samsung).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accuracy and completeness when describing prior art and other information
rubrics_metrics.description: Care should be taken to see that prior art or other information cited in a specification or in an IDS is properly described and not incorrectly or incompletely characterized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review applications prepared by others (e.g., foreign applicants); ensure foreign clients understand U.S. disclosure requirements; avoid submitting untranslated portions or partial translations that misdirect the examiner. The duty of candor does not require translating every foreign reference but refraining from submitting partial translations known to misdirect the examiner is required. See Apotex v. UCB, Semiconductor Energy Lab. case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inaccurate statements, misrepresentations, and mischaracterized experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce inaccurate statements, inaccurate evidence, or experiments into the record, either inadvertently or intentionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not state an experiment 'was run' when it was not; do not represent results as actual unless achieved; label prophetic examples clearly and separate them from working examples; use correct tense to distinguish actual vs predicted results. False statements in declarations can lead to unenforceability (Intellect Wireless v. HTC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on the examiner's awareness of related applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on the examiner of a particular application to be aware of other applications belonging to the same applicant or assignee; call such applications to the examiner's attention even if materiality is only questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lapse by the examiner does not excuse the applicant. Copending applications may be material even if they cannot result in a shorter patent term. See Dayco Prod. v. Total Containment and KangaROOS v. Caldor.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt, submit the information
rubrics_metrics.description: When in doubt about materiality, it is desirable and safest to submit information; the question of relevancy in close cases should be left to the examiner and not the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the attorney/agent/applicant does not consider the information necessarily material, someone else may see it differently and submitting avoids embarrassing issues. See U.S. Industries v. Norton and LaBounty Mfg. guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit information about prior uses and sales even if experimental or uncertain
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit information about prior uses and sales even if it appears they may have been experimental, not involve what is specifically claimed in the invention, or not encompass a completed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (TransWeb v. 3M, Hycor Corp. v. Schlueter Co., LaBounty) supports submitting such information; better to disclose and let the Office weigh materiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid submitting long lists of cumulative or marginally pertinent documents
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable to avoid submission of long lists of documents if it can be avoided; eliminate clearly irrelevant and marginally pertinent cumulative information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a long list is submitted, highlight or specifically bring to the applicant's attention those documents known to be most significant. Courts have criticized unnecessarily long or cumulative submissions (Penn Yan Boats v. Sea Lark Boats), though counterexamples exist (Molins PLC v. Textron).

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for continuation-in-part (CIP) related intervening material information
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for intervening material information or documents for CIP applications, particularly foreign patents and publications related to the parent application and dated more than one year before the filing date of the CIP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such intervening documents may be material. See In re Ruscetta, In re van Langenhoven, Chromalloy American Corp. v. Alloy Surfaces Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider potential prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. provisions when applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch out for information that might be deemed prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) and (g), which may be available under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 and affect patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-AIA 102(f) may be a prior art basis for 103; evidence under pre-AIA 102(g) may be relevant to 103. The AIA and continuity/priority issues mean pre-AIA provisions may apply to claims with effective filing dates before March 16, 2013 or to continuations/divisions/CIPs. Pre-AIA 103(c) disqualifies certain categories of prior art under specified circumstances. See cited cases and MPEP §§ 2146 - 2146.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure all individuals subject to the duty are informed and fulfill it
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure that all individuals who are subject to the duty of disclosure (as spelled out in 37 CFR 1.56) are informed of and fulfill their duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes inventors, attorneys, agents, and others involved in filing and prosecution. Record-keeping and proactive inquiries help ensure compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record reasons for discarding information as not material
rubrics_metrics.description: If information was specifically considered and discarded as not material, recording this fact and the reason in an attorney’s or applicant’s file may be helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such notes, while not required, can aid in explaining an honest and excusable mistake if allegations of fraud or inequitable conduct arise later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish materiality standard (37 CFR 1.56) from examiner's information requests (37 CFR 1.105)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 CFR 1.56, individuals have a duty to disclose information material to patentability. By contrast, 37 CFR 1.105 authorizes an examiner to require information reasonably necessary to examine or treat a matter, which can be a broader zone than materiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criteria for requiring information under 1.56 (materiality to patentability) is substantially higher than for 1.105 (reasonable necessity to examination). Examiner-required information under 1.105 may be relevant procedurally or substantively even if not material to patentability. See Star Fruits S.N.C. v. United States and Hyatt v. USPTO.
